# Exodus 28:1–22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter moves from the design of the tabernacle (chs. 25–27) to the men who will serve in it. The priestly garments are “holy garments,” set apart for sacred service, and their materials echo those of the tabernacle itself — gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen — linking the priest to the sanctuary where he ministers (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/exodus/28.htm). The chapter divides into instructions for preparing the garments (vv. 1–5), the ephod (vv. 6–14), the breastpiece (vv. 15–30), and then the robe, turban, tunic, and undergarments (vv. 31–43).

---

## v. 1 — The Calling of Aaron and His Sons

**“Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests.”**

- **Divine election, not human ambition.** David Guzik notes that the priesthood was “not earned by effort nor aspired to by ambition. It could only be inherited by birthright.” One must be born into the priestly family — a principle echoed in the New Covenant, where believers are priests through new birth into Christ’s family (1 Peter 2:5) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **Moses’ integrity.** John Gill observes that before this time every family head could offer sacrifice. Moses, whom Aben Ezra calls “a priest of priests,” does not seize the office for his own sons but bestows it on Aaron’s family — proof of his uprightness and lack of self-seeking (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **The Hebrew verb.** Precept Austin quotes the NET note: the verb is the Hiphil imperative of *qārav* (“to draw near”), carrying religious significance — to present someone to God as an offering (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **Priestly mediation.** The Hebrew verb *kāhan* (“to minister as priest”) occurs 23 times in the OT, always denoting mediation between the divine and the ordinary. NIDOTTE (cited at Precept Austin) says: “Perhaps the central concept of priesthood is mediation between the sphere of the divine and the ordinary world” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** adds that these men were “consecrated for the ministry of the priesthood” with garments specially designed to mark their office as holy and separate (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-28.html).

---

## v. 2 — Holy Garments for Glory and Beauty

**“Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor.”**

- **“For glory and for beauty.”** Guzik says: “Since there was something glorious and beautiful — indeed, heavenly about the priestly service, it was appropriate to make the garments glorious and beautiful” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **Exalting the office.** The NET note (at Precept Austin) explains that the Hebrew *lĕkābôd ûlĕtipʾāret* means “for glory and for beauty.” W.C. Kaiser notes these clothes were “to exalt the office of the high priest as well as beautify the worship of God” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **Against heathen nakedness.** Gill points out that some pagan priests performed their rites naked, a shameful practice. In opposition, God commanded His priests to be clothed splendidly. The garments typify “the glory and beauty of Christ’s human nature” and “the garments of salvation, and robe of righteousness, in which all his people, his priests, appear exceeding glorious and beautiful” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **A pointed critique.** Adam Clarke (quoted by both Guzik and Precept Austin) asked of clerical dress: “Is then the dismal black, now worn by almost all kinds of priests and ministers, for glory and for beauty? Is it emblematic of any thing that is good, glorious, or excellent?” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

---

## v. 3 — Skilled Craftsmen Filled with the Spirit of Wisdom

**“You are to instruct all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, to make garments for Aaron’s consecration, so that he may serve Me as priest.”**

- **The Spirit’s gifting for practical work.** Guzik emphasizes: “If it is really done to the glory of God, practical, manual service requires the leading of the Holy Spirit just as much as what we normally consider to be spiritual service” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **“Wise of heart.”** The NET note (at Precept Austin) explains that the Hebrew *ḥakmê* (“wise”) has as its basic meaning “skill” or “skillful.” The “heart” for Hebrews is the locus of understanding, mind, and will. To be “wise of heart” meant they had the understanding to do skillful work (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **Learned in Egypt.** Cole (quoted by both Guzik and Precept Austin) notes that “The Hebrew slaves must have learned many Egyptian arts and crafts, such as metalwork, spinning, weaving and embroidery during their stay in Egypt” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **“To consecrate him.”** Gill explains that the garments themselves were part of Aaron’s consecration: “for the priests, without having these garments on, might not minister in their office; for when these garments were off, as they were when they were out of their service, they were as other men, as laymen” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **The priority of ministry to God.** Precept Austin notes that three times in vv. 1–4 the phrase “that he may minister to Me as priest” appears. The priest’s first ministry is to God Himself, not to the people (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

---

## v. 4 — The Six Garments Listed

**“These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash.”**

- **The high priest’s distinctive garments.** Ellicott notes that “the garments peculiar to the high priest are taken first, and described with great elaboration in thirty-six verses (4–39)” — breastplate, ephod, robe of the ephod, mitre (turban), linen tunic with girdle, and linen drawers (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm). (The drawers appear in vv. 42–43.)

- **Seven parts.** Thompson (at Precept Austin) counts seven parts to the high-priestly garment. Precept Austin notes that the key word throughout this introduction is “to minister as priest to Me” — the priority is to God, not the people (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **The “woven tunic.”** The Hebrew word *tashbets* (translated “checkered” or “broidered” in older versions) appears only here. The NET note says its meaning is uncertain; it may mean a tunic “shaped by sewing … so that it will fit tightly around the body” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **Christological reading.** Multiple sources read each garment typologically. Grant’s Commentary says: “Aaron, the high priest, is typical of Christ, our Great High Priest, and his sons are typical of believers today in their priestly character” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-28.html).

---

## v. 5 — The Materials

**“They shall use gold, along with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.”**

- **Same materials as the tabernacle.** Ellicott observes that the materials are “the same as those employed for the vail and curtains of the sanctuary (Exodus 26:1, 31, 36), but with the further addition of gold and precious stones” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm). This identifies the priest with the sacred place where he serves.

- **Mystical significance.** Gill says the materials “had a mystical significance in them.” Gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen in the ephod and breastplate emblematically represent the glory, heavenly origin, royalty, blood/sacrifice, and purity of Christ (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **Linen as noble dress.** Cole notes that “linen was the dress of the noble and the priest in Egypt, chosen both for coolness and cleanliness” (quoted at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

---

## vv. 6–8 — The Ephod: Construction

**v. 6: “They are to make the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.”**

- **What was the ephod?** Guzik describes it as “essentially an ornate apron-like garment.” Gill describes it as the outermost garment, a short piece reaching to the loins or buttocks (citing Kimchi and Abarbinel), covering back and breast, girt about with a curious girdle. It had no sleeves (contra Josephus) (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **A type of Christ’s human nature.** Gill writes that the ephod “was a symbol of the human nature of Christ, our great High Priest … a fit emblem of the glory, excellency, and purity of Christ’s human nature; of the various graces of the Spirit in it; of his heavenly original; of his blood, sufferings, and death, and glorious exaltation; and of its being a curious piece of workmanship wrought by the Lord himself, Hebrews 10:5” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **The Catholic Encyclopedia** describes three parts to the ephod: (1) a kind of waistcoat or bodice (the main part), (2) two shoulder-pieces or suspenders, and (3) a girdle (cincture), all of fine-twisted linen embroidered with violet, purple, scarlet, and gold (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05497a.htm).

**v. 7: “It shall have two shoulder pieces attached at two of its corners, so it can be fastened.”**

- Ellicott explains the ephod was made in two pieces (front and back), joined at the shoulders “apparently by a seam” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm). Gill notes the shoulder pieces met on the shoulders and were buttoned with the two onyx stones.

**v. 8: “And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod must be of one piece, of the same workmanship…”**

- The waistband (translated “curious girdle” in KJV) was woven in one piece with the ephod, not a separate piece sewn on. Gill says it “went out from it like two thongs … which girt the ephod close to the back and breast” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm). Ellicott notes the Hebrew *khēsheb* means properly “device” or “ornamental work,” but Josephus confirms it was in fact a girdle (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm).

- Grant’s Commentary sees the gold in the ephod as signifying that Christ “must Himself be God” (Hebrews 1), while the blue, purple, scarlet, and linen speak of His unique manhood — heavenly (blue), kingly (purple), servant (scarlet), and morally pure (fine linen) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-28.html).

---

## vv. 9–12 — The Onyx Stones on the Shoulders

**v. 9: “Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel.”**

- Gill notes the stones are called “onyx” from the colour of a man’s nail. The Targums call them beryl; the Septuagint, emerald; Josephus, sardonyx. The stones must have been large to have six full names engraved on each. Gill mentions an oriental onyx in the Dresden Museum measuring almost six inches in diameter (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

**v. 10: “Six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth.”**

- Gill lists the traditional order: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali on the right shoulder; Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin on the left (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

**v. 11: “Engrave the names of the sons of Israel on the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal.”**

- The engraving was cut deep, like a signet (seal), so that impressions would stand out. Gill notes this shows “engraving on precious stones is very old, and the ancients indeed are said to excel in this art” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

**v. 12: “Fasten both stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD.”**

- **“Memorial stones.”** Ellicott clarifies: the stones were “stones of memorial” *to God on behalf of Israel* — to remind God that the high priest represented all the tribes and pleaded before Him in their name (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm).

- **Bearing on the shoulders.** Guzik explains the shoulders are “a place of work; therefore, in the priest’s ministry unto the LORD, he also worked for and with the people.” Cole adds: “Aaron bears Israel’s names before God whenever he enters the Tent, identifying himself with them” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **Typology of Christ.** Gill sees here a type of Christ who “presents all his people to his divine Father, makes intercession for them, and bears all their burdens, the care and government of them being upon his shoulders, Isaiah 9:6” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm). The Church Pulpit Commentary similarly says: “Aaron bearing the names of the people before the Lord on his ephod is a picture of Christ bearing the names of His people in holy remembrance before God” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/exodus-28.html).

---

## vv. 13–14 — Gold Filigree Settings and Chains

**v. 13: “Fashion gold filigree settings.”**

- Gill sees these as the sockets (bezels) to hold the onyx stones, mentioned again here “because of the chains to be fastened to them” in the next verse (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

**v. 14: “And two chains of pure gold, made of braided cord work; and attach these chains to the settings.”**

- The chains connected the breastpiece to the shoulder stones. Gill explains: “one end of them was fastened to rings on the ouches in the shoulder pieces, and the other end to rings on the breastplate, and thus it hung.” The chains were not linked rings but “golden wires twisted together as a rope is twisted” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

---

## vv. 15–16 — The Breastpiece of Judgment: Design

**v. 15: “You are also to make a breastpiece of judgment with the same workmanship as the ephod.”**

- **“Breastpiece of judgment.”** The Hebrew *ḥōšen mišpāṭ* is rendered in the Septuagint as *logion* (“oracle”) and in the Vulgate as *rationale* (“rational”). The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the original meaning of the Hebrew term has been lost; Ewald proposed “the pouch of the Oracle” (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11600b.htm).

- **Why “of judgment”?** StudyLight.org (citing Dummelow) explains it was called the breastplate of judgment because it held the Urim and Thummim, the means by which God’s “judgments” (decisions) were declared (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/28-15.html). Gill adds it reminded the high priest “that he should do justice and judgment in the execution of his office” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

- **The Hebrew word *ḥōšen*.** Ellicott notes the etymology is uncertain, but “pouch would convey a much clearer idea of what is intended” than “breastplate,” since v. 30 shows it was a container (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/28-15.htm).

**v. 16: “It must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide.”**

- **A doubled square.** When folded, it was a span (about 9 inches / half a cubit) each way. Gill says the full length before folding was a cubit (two spans). The doubling was likely to make it strong enough to bear the weight of the precious stones, not necessarily to create a pocket — though many traditions hold the Urim and Thummim were placed inside (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm). Dummelow says it was “really a pouch” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-28.html).

- **Squareness.** Gill links this to the New Jerusalem, also foursquare (Revelation 21:16), “denoting the perfection, firmness, and immovableness” of the church (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm).

---

## vv. 17–20 — The Four Rows of Gemstones

**v. 17: first row — ruby (sardius), topaz, emerald (carbuncle).**
**v. 18: second row — turquoise, sapphire, diamond.**
**v. 19: third row — jacinth (ligure), agate, amethyst.**
**v. 20: fourth row — beryl, onyx, jasper.**

- **Uncertain identifications.** Guzik states plainly: “It is impossible to know exactly what all of these gemstones were.” The Expositor’s Bible Commentary (at StudyLight) adds: “All attempts to derive edification from the nature of these jewels must be governed by the commonplace reflection that we cannot identify them; and many of the present names are incorrect. It is almost certain that neither topaz, sapphire nor diamond could have been engraved, as these stones were” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-28.html).

- **Connection to Revelation.** Guzik notes that Revelation 21:19–20 describes the foundations of the New Jerusalem with a series of twelve gemstones, which may correspond to the stones in the breastplate — linking priestly ministry to future glory (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **Preciousness of God’s people.** Guzik observes: “We cannot neglect the fact God commanded the tribes to have their names inscribed on gemstones — truly precious things. God’s people are indeed precious to Him” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

- **Catholic enumeration.** The Catholic Encyclopedia names them: carnelian (sardius), chrysolite (topaz), emerald; turquoise, sapphire (lapis lazuli), moonstone (diamond); jacinth, agate, amethyst; beryl, onyx, jasper. The NRSV Catholic Edition follows a similar identification (https://biblehub.com/nrsvce/exodus/28.htm).

---

## v. 21 — Inscribed with the Names of the Twelve Tribes

**“The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.”**

- **Individual engraving.** Each stone bore the name of one tribe, engraved like a signet. The tribes were doubly represented in the high priest’s costume — on the shoulder stones (vv. 9–12) and on the breastpiece stones (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm).

- **Shoulders and heart.** Guzik draws the key distinction: “It was not enough that the High Priest worked for the people (having them on his shoulders). He must also love the people — that is, bear them on his heart … It isn’t enough for a priest to have a heart for God. He must also have a heart for the people” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary echoes this: shoulders signify burden-bearing, the breastpiece over the heart signifies they are “beloved of God” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-28.html).

- **Christological type.** The Church Pulpit Commentary says: “The breastplate teaches that Christ not only bears His people on His shoulders for strength, but lays them separately on His heart for love” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/exodus-28.html).

---

## v. 22 — The Braided Chains for the Breastpiece

**“For the breastpiece, make braided chains like cords of pure gold.”**

- These chains (repeating the design of v. 14) were to attach the breastpiece to the ephod at the shoulder settings. Dummelow notes the RV translates “chains like cords, of wreathen work” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-28.html). The chains ensured the breastpiece was securely fastened and would not swing loose (v. 28), keeping the names of Israel always over the high priest’s heart.

- **Unity of the garment.** Guzik notes the gold chains “attach the breastpiece, forming a unified garment that speaks of unity among the tribes” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On Exodus 28:1–22, the differences between Protestant traditions are largely matters of **emphasis** rather than outright doctrinal conflict:

1. **Typological emphasis (Reformed/Baptist):** Reformed and Baptist commentators such as Gill and Grant’s Commentary heavily emphasize the typology of Christ in every detail. Gill sees the ephod as a “symbol of the human nature of Christ,” the gold as His deity, the fine linen as His purity, and the onyx stones as Christ bearing His people’s names before the Father (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/28.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-28.html). This Christ-centered typological reading is the dominant traditional Protestant approach.

2. **Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis (Enduring Word):** David Guzik’s commentary, while sharing the Christ-typology, gives particular attention to the Holy Spirit’s role — noting that the “spirit of wisdom” given to artisans (v. 3) represents a genuine gifting of the Holy Spirit for practical, manual work, not merely a natural skill (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-28/).

3. **Baptist emphasis on the priesthood of all believers:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary and Precept Austin both draw a direct line from the OT priesthood to 1 Peter 2:5, 9 — emphasizing that under the New Covenant every believer is a priest. Precept Austin stresses this repeatedly, quoting Peter’s “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

4. **Lutheran:** No distinctly Lutheran commentary on these verses was found within the permitted search sources (lcms.org, 1517.org).

5. **Methodist/Wesleyan:** No distinctly Methodist or Wesleyan commentary was found within the permitted sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com).

6. **Anglican:** Ellicott’s commentary (standard Anglican reference) offers careful historical-grammatical notes, focusing on the Hebrew terminology, the structure of the garments, and archaeological parallels, while remaining more restrained on extended typological interpretation (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/28.htm).

---

## Catholic and Orthodox Views

- **Catholic (New Advent / Catholic Encyclopedia):** The Catholic Encyclopedia provides detailed descriptions of the ephod, breastplate (“rational of judgment”), and the Urim and Thummim, following the Vulgate terminology. It notes the ephod was not the high priest’s ordinary garb but was worn specifically while performing ministerial duties and consulting the Lord. The breastplate is called the *rationale* in the Vulgate (from the Septuagint’s *logion*, “oracle”). The Catholic Encyclopedia also discusses the “common ephod” worn by Samuel and David (linen only, without the colours) and the “idolatrous ephod” made by Gideon (Judges 8:26–27) (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05497a.htm; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11600b.htm).

- **Orthodox (OCA):** No results were found within the permitted Orthodox source (oca.org).

---

## Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes** (cited via Precept Austin): The NET notes offer lexical precision. For example, v. 3’s “spirit of wisdom” is explained: “There is no necessity to take this as a reference to the Holy Spirit who produces wisdom in these people, although that is not totally impossible.” The word “spirit” (*rûaḥ*) probably refers to their “attitude and ability.” Cassuto renders it: “to all the artisans skilled in the making of stately robes, in the heart [i.e., mind] of each of whom I have implanted sagacity in his craft” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-28-commentary).

- **The Expositor’s Bible Commentary** (at StudyLight) is cautious about over-interpreting the gemstones: “All attempts to derive edification from the nature of these jewels must be governed by the commonplace reflection that we cannot identify them” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-28.html).

- **Urim and Thummim.** Constable’s Expository Notes (at StudyLight) relays Youngblood’s view: “The phrase ‘Urim and Thummim’ is best translated into English as ‘curses and perfections,’ meaning that if ‘Urim’ dominated when the lots were cast the answer would be no but if ‘Thummim’ dominated the answer would be yes” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-28.html). This reflects the prevalent modern scholarly view that they were sacred lots.

- **bibleodyssey.org:** No results were found within search constraints.

---

## Summary of Major Themes Across Traditions

| Symbol | Traditional Reading |
|---|---|
| Ephod | Christ’s human nature and priestly office; beauty, glory, heavenly origin |
| Shoulder stones | Christ bearing His people’s burdens; intercession; governmental care |
| Breastpiece over heart | Christ’s love for His people; individual remembrance |
| Twelve gemstones | The twelve tribes — God’s people as precious to Him; unity and diversity |
| Gold chains | The secure, unbreakable bond between Christ’s heart and His people |
| “Holiness to the LORD” (v. 36) | Christ’s perfect holiness imputed to believers |
